interview.q: What does the universal selector match, and why avoid it for styling?
interview.answer: An asterisk matches every element, so a styling rule reaches places you did not consider; it is useful in a reset but too broad for component design.

interview.q: What does a type selector match?
interview.answer: Every element with that tag name, regardless of class or position, which makes it a good base rule and a poor way to style one instance.

interview.q: How does a class selector match when an element has several classes?
interview.answer: It matches when the element's class attribute contains that exact token, so an element can satisfy several independent class rules at once.

interview.q: Why can an element carry more than one class?
interview.answer: Classes compose: one supplies layout, another colour, another state, so behaviour can be combined without inventing a new selector for every combination.

interview.q: Why is styling through IDs a problem?
interview.answer: An ID is unique, cannot be reused across components, and carries specificity high enough that later variations need heavier selectors to override it.

interview.q: What happens when one selector in a comma list is invalid?
interview.answer: For an ordinary selector list the whole rule is dropped, because the browser cannot know which part of the list you meant.

interview.q: How does the descendant combinator differ from the child combinator?
interview.answer: A space matches an ancestor at any depth; a greater-than sign matches only an element whose direct parent is the named one.

interview.q: When is a child combinator the safer choice?
interview.answer: When a component's styles must not leak into nested copies of the same markup, since only the immediate children are affected.

interview.q: What does the adjacent sibling combinator match?
interview.answer: The one element that immediately follows the first, with no other element between them, such as a label directly after an input.

interview.q: What does the general sibling combinator match?
interview.answer: Every following sibling that matches the selector, not only the first, which is useful for a heading followed by several paragraphs.

interview.q: How do you select an element that merely has an attribute?
interview.answer: Write the attribute name in brackets, such as [disabled], which matches any element carrying that attribute whatever its value.

interview.q: How do you select an exact attribute value?
interview.answer: Use the equals form, such as [type="email"], which matches only when the value is exactly that string.

interview.q: What does the prefix attribute selector do?
interview.answer: [href^="https"] matches values that begin with the given text, which is a common way to mark external links.

interview.q: What does the suffix attribute selector do?
interview.answer: [href$=".pdf"] matches values that end with the text, useful for marking file types without adding another class.

interview.q: What does the substring attribute selector do?
interview.answer: [class*="promo"] matches any value containing that sequence, which is broad and should be used only when the naming is controlled.

interview.q: What does the i flag change in an attribute selector?
interview.answer: It makes the value comparison ASCII case-insensitive, so [type="EMAIL" i] also matches type="email".

interview.q: What is the difference between a pseudo-class and a pseudo-element?
interview.answer: A pseudo-class selects an element in a state or position; a pseudo-element selects or generates a part of an element, such as its first line.

interview.q: What does :not() do?
interview.answer: It excludes elements that match its argument, and it can be chained or given a complex list in modern browsers.

interview.q: How does :is() choose its specificity?
interview.answer: It takes the specificity of the most specific selector in its argument list, so it can unexpectedly raise the weight of a rule.

interview.q: Why use :where() instead of :is()?
interview.answer: :where() always contributes zero specificity, which makes it ideal for resets and base styles that must not outrank component rules.

interview.q: What problem does :has() solve?
interview.answer: It lets a selector depend on a descendant or following sibling, so a parent can be styled because of a child's state without adding a class from script.

interview.q: How does :nth-child() count elements?
interview.answer: It counts an element's position among all of its element siblings, so other types of siblings affect the result.

interview.q: How is :nth-of-type() different?
interview.answer: It counts only siblings of the same element type, so intervening paragraphs do not change which heading is selected.

interview.q: When does :first-child match?
interview.answer: Only when the element is the first element child of its parent; a text node before it does not count, but another element does.

interview.q: What does :only-child match?
interview.answer: An element that is the sole element child of its parent, which is useful for layouts with one item instead of several.

interview.q: What does :empty match, and what is the common surprise?
interview.answer: It matches an element with no children or text at all, and even a single whitespace character counts as text, so the element stops matching.

interview.q: What is :root and how is it different from html?
interview.answer: :root matches the document's root element and has class-level specificity, while the type selector html has element-level specificity.

interview.q: What specificity does :has() contribute?
interview.answer: It takes the specificity of its most specific argument, the same rule as :is(), so a complex argument raises the weight of the whole selector.

interview.q: Why does one invalid selector break a whole selector list?
interview.answer: Without forgiving syntax the parser cannot decide which list item you intended, so it discards the rule rather than applying a partial match.

interview.q: Are complex selectors actually slow?
interview.answer: Modern engines match right-to-left and optimise common cases, so readability and correctness matter far more than micro-optimising selector length.

interview.q: Why avoid styling with IDs even when the markup has them?
interview.answer: IDs cannot repeat, so the style cannot be reused, and their weight makes every variation a specificity fight instead of a class change.

interview.q: What does BEM encode in a class name?
interview.answer: A block, its elements with a double underscore, and modifiers with a double hyphen, so ownership and variation are readable from the markup.

interview.q: Which attribute selectors are useful for form controls?
interview.answer: [type="email"], [required], [disabled] and [aria-invalid="true"] let CSS react to real control state without extra classes.

interview.q: What does :lang() select?
interview.answer: Elements whose language matches the given value, including inherited language, so typography can change for a quoted foreign phrase.

interview.q: What does :dir() select?
interview.answer: Elements whose directionality is left-to-right or right-to-left, which is useful for logical layout in bilingual documents.

interview.q: What does :target match?
interview.answer: The element whose ID matches the URL fragment, which lets a page highlight the section a link jumped to.

interview.q: What is :scope for?
interview.answer: It refers to the element a selector is scoped to, such as the root of querySelectorAll or a nested style scope.

interview.q: What does & mean inside a nested CSS rule?
interview.answer: It stands for the parent selector, so & .child or &:hover builds the full selector without repeating the parent by hand.

interview.q: What is the specificity of .nav a:hover?
interview.answer: Two class-level components and one element component, written 0-2-1, because .nav and :hover each count as a class.

interview.q: What is the specificity of #id .class?
interview.answer: One ID and one class, written 1-1-0, so it beats any number of classes without an ID.

interview.q: Why does duplicating selectors hurt maintenance?
interview.answer: Each copy drifts independently, and adding a variation means finding every duplicate or raising specificity until the newest rule wins.

interview.q: How do you debug a selector that matches nothing?
interview.answer: Inspect the element, check the selector text against the DOM, confirm class case, and test the rule in the Styles panel before assuming the CSS file is wrong.

interview.q: What does :has() change about CSS architecture?
interview.answer: It allows state to flow upward from a child, which removes some classes that script used to add, but it should be treated as an enhancement where support matters.

interview.q: How does a three-digit hex colour expand?
interview.answer: Each digit is doubled, so #f0a becomes #ff00aa; the shorthand is valid only when both digits of every pair are identical.

interview.q: What does an eight-digit hex colour add?
interview.answer: The final pair is alpha, so #2563ebcc is the blue #2563eb at roughly eighty percent opacity.

interview.q: What is the space-separated rgb() syntax?
interview.answer: It writes channels without commas and puts alpha after a slash, such as rgb(37 99 235 / 0.8), which is the modern form.

interview.q: How is hsl() written?
interview.answer: Hue in degrees, saturation and lightness as percentages, with optional alpha after a slash, such as hsl(221 83% 53% / 0.9).

interview.q: What does the color() function allow?
interview.answer: It selects an explicit colour space, such as display-p3, which can express colours outside the sRGB gamut on capable displays.

interview.q: Why use oklch() instead of hsl()?
interview.answer: OKLCH is perceptually uniform, so changing lightness or hue behaves more predictably and a palette keeps even contrast steps.

interview.q: What does color-mix() do?
interview.answer: It blends two colours in a chosen colour space, which is useful for deriving hover or tint variants from a single token.

interview.q: What is the difference between opacity and an alpha colour?
interview.answer: opacity fades the whole element including its children and border, while an alpha colour fades only that one paint.

interview.q: What does currentColor refer to?
interview.answer: It resolves to the element's computed color, so a border or icon can follow the text colour without repeating the value.

interview.q: Is transparent the same as a transparent black?
interview.answer: transparent is a named colour equal to transparent black, but using it as a background can still change how blending and shadows behave.

interview.q: Why are named colours risky for a design system?
interview.answer: Names are limited and inconsistent across palettes, so a brand token expressed as a name is harder to adjust and version than a value.

interview.q: What is a contrast ratio?
interview.answer: A ratio between the relative luminance of two colours, from 1:1 to 21:1, used to judge whether text is readable against its background.

interview.q: What contrast does WCAG AA require for normal text?
interview.answer: At least 4.5:1 for normal-size text, measured between the text colour and the actual background behind it.

interview.q: What contrast is required for large text?
interview.answer: At least 3:1, because larger glyphs remain legible at a lower ratio than body-size text.

interview.q: What does background-color set?
interview.answer: The solid colour painted behind an element's content and padding, below any background image and inside the border box.

interview.q: How do multiple background images stack?
interview.answer: The first layer in the list paints on top, and later layers paint beneath it, so an overlay gradient is written before the photo.

interview.q: What does background-repeat control?
interview.answer: Whether and how an image tiles across the background; no-repeat shows one copy, while repeat-x or repeat-y tiles in one direction.

interview.q: What is the difference between background-size cover and contain?
interview.answer: cover fills the box and may crop the image, while contain shows the whole image and may leave empty space.

interview.q: What does background-position do?
interview.answer: It places the image within the painting area, using keywords, lengths or percentages, often combined with cover to choose the crop focus.

interview.q: What does background-attachment: fixed do?
interview.answer: It fixes the background to the viewport so it does not move with the element's scroll, an effect that is often expensive on mobile.

interview.q: Why is the background shorthand dangerous after setting a colour?
interview.answer: It resets every background longhand it owns, so a later shorthand without a colour can wipe the colour you set earlier.

interview.q: How do you set the direction of a linear gradient?
interview.answer: Use an angle or a side keyword, such as linear-gradient(135deg, ...) or linear-gradient(to right, ...), before the colour stops.

interview.q: How is a radial gradient positioned?
interview.answer: Its centre and shape are set before the stops, such as radial-gradient(circle at 30% 30%, ...), which changes where the colour bloom begins.

interview.q: What is a conic gradient useful for?
interview.answer: It sweeps colour around a centre point, which suits pie charts, colour wheels and angular progress indicators.

interview.q: What is a colour stop?
interview.answer: A colour paired with an optional position along the gradient line, which tells the browser where that colour must be reached.

interview.q: What is a hard stop in a gradient?
interview.answer: Two stops at the same position create an abrupt edge instead of a blend, which can draw stripes or a sharp split background.

interview.q: When do you use a repeating gradient?
interview.answer: When a small pattern must tile across a larger area, such as stripes or a progress track, using repeating-linear-gradient with a short cycle.

interview.q: Why does a gradient sometimes show banding?
interview.answer: Too few colour steps across a large area reveal the 8-bit quantization, which can be reduced with subtle noise, dithering or a smoother colour space.

interview.q: How do you place text over a photo reliably?
interview.answer: Paint a semi-transparent gradient or solid overlay as the top background layer, then choose a text colour that contrasts with the darkest part of that overlay.

interview.q: Why set a background colour when using a background image?
interview.answer: If the image fails or loads slowly, the fallback colour keeps the text on a deliberate surface instead of the browser default.

interview.q: What does background-blend-mode do?
interview.answer: It blends an element's background layers with each other, such as multiplying a texture into a colour, without affecting the content above them.

interview.q: How is filter different from backdrop-filter?
interview.answer: filter affects the element's own rendering, while backdrop-filter blurs or adjusts whatever is painted behind the element.

interview.q: How do you design colours for dark mode?
interview.answer: Define semantic tokens, then override their values in a dark scope; pure inversion is avoided because saturated colours and shadows behave differently on dark surfaces.

interview.q: What are CSS system colours?
interview.answer: Keywords such as Canvas and CanvasText that follow the user's operating-system theme, which help a page fit forced-colours and high-contrast modes.

interview.q: What is forced-colors mode?
interview.answer: A user setting where the browser replaces author colours with a limited system palette, so designs must keep borders, focus and meaning visible without colour alone.

interview.q: Why does print need different colour decisions?
interview.answer: Printers handle ink and paper differently, backgrounds are often not printed, and light text on a dark background can become unreadable or waste ink.

interview.q: What is colour management in CSS?
interview.answer: The browser maps declared colours into the display's colour space, which is why a wide-gamut P3 colour can look different from the same sRGB value.

interview.q: Why keep a palette of raw colour tokens?
interview.answer: A small named palette gives one place to adjust values, while components reference semantic tokens built from it instead of inventing new hex codes.

interview.q: What is a semantic colour token?
interview.answer: A name that describes a role, such as surface or danger, rather than a hue, so the value can change with theme while the meaning stays stable.

interview.q: Which tools help verify contrast?
interview.answer: Browser DevTools' contrast readout, dedicated contrast checkers and automated accessibility audits, always measured against the real rendered background.

interview.q: How do you make gradient text?
interview.answer: Clip the background to the text and make the text transparent, but keep a solid fallback because the technique can fail in forced-colours or older engines.

interview.q: Why can large background images hurt performance?
interview.answer: They add download and decode cost, and a fixed or repainting background can force expensive work during scroll, especially on mobile GPUs.

interview.q: Why is colour alone a poor way to convey meaning?
interview.answer: Readers with colour-vision deficiency, monochrome screens or forced-colours mode lose the distinction, so pair colour with text, icons, weight or pattern.

interview.q: What is a CSS pixel?
interview.answer: A logical unit resolved against the display's reference pixel, not a guarantee of one physical device pixel, which is why high-density screens scale it.

interview.q: What does rem measure?
interview.answer: The root element's computed font size, so one rem follows the user's base size instead of a hard-coded pixel value.

interview.q: What does em measure?
interview.answer: The element's own computed font size, or its parent's when used on font-size, which makes it relative and sometimes compounding.

interview.q: A percentage width resolves against what?
interview.answer: The containing block's width, so the same fifty percent is a different number of pixels in a narrow and a wide parent.

interview.q: When are vw and vh useful?
interview.answer: For sizes that should follow the viewport, such as a full-height hero or fluid type, though vw includes the scrollbar on desktop.

interview.q: What do dvh, svh and lvh solve?
interview.answer: They separate the dynamic, small and large viewport heights on mobile, where browser chrome changes the visible area during scroll.

interview.q: When do vmin and vmax help?
interview.answer: When a square or shape must follow the shorter or longer viewport side, so it stays proportional in both portrait and landscape.

interview.q: What does the ch unit represent?
interview.answer: The width of the zero glyph in the current font, which makes it a useful approximation for limiting a line to a number of characters.

interview.q: What does ex measure?
interview.answer: The x-height of the current font, a font-relative unit that is rarely used except for small optical adjustments.

interview.q: What does fr mean in a grid track?
interview.answer: A fraction of the free space left after fixed tracks and gaps, so 1fr and 2fr split that space in a one-to-two ratio.

interview.q: Which CSS units are absolute?
interview.answer: px, cm, mm, in, pt and pc are absolute in CSS terms, though px is still resolved against the reference pixel rather than a device dot.

interview.q: When are physical units such as cm or pt still appropriate?
interview.answer: For print stylesheets and documents that must match paper dimensions, not for screen layout where zoom and density vary.

interview.q: What is the default root font size?
interview.answer: Sixteen CSS pixels in most browsers, but it is a user preference, so rem-based layouts must not assume that number is fixed.

interview.q: How does browser zoom interact with px and rem?
interview.answer: Zoom scales the whole layout, but a user's font-size preference changes the root size, which rem respects and px ignores for text.

interview.q: Why does nested em sizing compound?
interview.answer: Each level multiplies its parent's computed size, so two nested 1.2em elements produce 1.44 times the outer size instead of 1.2.

interview.q: Why is line-height better left unitless?
interview.answer: A unitless value multiplies the element's own font size, so nested text keeps the intended ratio instead of inheriting a fixed length.

interview.q: What does calc() require around plus and minus?
interview.answer: Whitespace on both sides of the operator, because without it the parser can read the sign as part of a number or identifier.

interview.q: What does min() choose?
interview.answer: The smallest of its arguments, allowing a width to shrink below a preferred value but never exceed a hard limit.

interview.q: What does max() choose?
interview.answer: The largest of its arguments, which is useful for a minimum size that still grows with available space.

interview.q: What are the three parts of clamp()?
interview.answer: A minimum, a preferred value and a maximum; the browser returns the preferred value bounded by the other two.

interview.q: What does minmax() do in a grid track?
interview.answer: It sets a track's minimum and maximum size, so a column can shrink no further than the first value and grow no larger than the second.

interview.q: How does fit-content behave?
interview.answer: It sizes to the content up to a limit, then stops growing, which is useful for chips and sidebars that should not stretch.

interview.q: What does auto mean for width and height?
interview.answer: It lets the browser resolve the size from the layout context, such as filling a block or sizing to content, rather than a fixed number.

interview.q: Why is zero allowed without a unit?
interview.answer: Zero is the same length in every unit, so the specification permits the bare number while other nonzero lengths require a unit.

interview.q: What does percentage padding resolve against?
interview.answer: The containing block's inline size, even for vertical padding, which is why percentage padding can create surprising aspect ratios.

interview.q: Why does percentage height often fail?
interview.answer: It needs a definite containing block height; if the parent's height is auto, the percentage has nothing to resolve against and is treated as auto.

interview.q: What does aspect-ratio do?
interview.answer: It sets a preferred width-to-height ratio, letting one dimension follow the other while the box remains responsive.

interview.q: What are container query units?
interview.answer: Units such as cqw and cqh that resolve against the nearest query container instead of the viewport, so a component can scale with its own space.

interview.q: Can media queries use rem?
interview.answer: Yes, and doing so ties breakpoints to the user's root font size, so a reader who enlarges text gets the layout intended for a wider screen.

interview.q: Why keep borders in px?
interview.answer: A one-pixel border usually expresses a hairline regardless of text size, while spacing and type should follow the user's scale.

interview.q: What are resolution units used for?
interview.answer: dpi, dpcm and dppx describe pixel density, mainly in media queries for choosing sharper images on high-density displays.

interview.q: What are angle units used for?
interview.answer: deg, grad, rad and turn describe rotation and gradient direction, with turn being a convenient full circle.

interview.q: What are time units used for?
interview.answer: s and ms set transition and animation durations and delays; they are the only units accepted for those properties.

interview.q: Why prefer fr over percentages in a grid?
interview.answer: fr distributes the space left after gaps and fixed tracks, so tracks do not overflow when gaps are added.

interview.q: Why are viewport units unreliable for mobile height?
interview.answer: Mobile browser chrome changes the visible height during scroll, so vh can be taller than the actual visible area; dvh or svh reflect that behaviour.

interview.q: How do you create fluid type?
interview.answer: Use clamp() with a viewport-relative preferred value, bounded by a readable minimum and maximum, instead of fixing a size per breakpoint.

interview.q: How do you create fluid spacing?
interview.answer: Use clamp() or calc() on a spacing token, so gaps grow with the viewport within limits rather than jumping at breakpoints.

interview.q: How do you convert between px and rem?
interview.answer: Divide the pixel value by the root font size, usually sixteen, so 24px becomes 1.5rem; the conversion is a design aid, not a runtime rule.

interview.q: Why can a px-based design fail accessibility?
interview.answer: The text ignores the reader's font-size preference, so a user who enlarges text still sees the original size and may be unable to read it.

interview.q: Why use rem for spacing as well as text?
interview.answer: Spacing tied to the root scale keeps the rhythm proportional when the reader changes text size, instead of leaving cramped gaps around larger type.

interview.q: Why is ch useful for a reading measure?
interview.answer: A width in ch approximates characters per line, so a 65ch limit keeps a comfortable measure even when the font size changes.

interview.q: How do you debug a unit mismatch?
interview.answer: Inspect the Computed panel for the resolved pixel value, then trace which parent or font size the relative unit resolved against.

interview.q: Which unit should a beginner default to?
interview.answer: rem for type and spacing, percentages or fr for layout, and px for hairlines, then reach for viewport and container units only when the layout needs them.

interview.q: Why does font-family take an ordered stack?
interview.answer: The browser uses the first family it can render, so the order decides which available font wins before the generic fallback is reached.

interview.q: Why must every stack end in a generic family?
interview.answer: A generic family is guaranteed to exist, so the page still gets a sensible serif, sans-serif or monospace instead of the browser's arbitrary default.

interview.q: What is a web font?
interview.answer: A font file delivered by the page and declared with @font-face, which gives a consistent typeface instead of relying on installed fonts.

interview.q: What does @font-face declare?
interview.answer: A font family name, one or more sources with formats, and descriptors such as weight, style and display behaviour.

interview.q: What does font-display control?
interview.answer: How a web font behaves while it loads: swap shows fallback text immediately, block hides text briefly, and optional avoids late swaps.

interview.q: Why preload a font file?
interview.answer: Preloading starts the request before the CSS that references it is parsed, which reduces the delay before the first text paint.

interview.q: What is a flash of invisible text?
interview.answer: A period where the browser hides text while waiting for a web font, usually caused by a block period in font-display.

interview.q: What do numeric font-weight values mean?
interview.answer: They range from 100 to 900 in increasing boldness, and a variable font can interpolate between them instead of jumping to named weights.

interview.q: What is a variable font?
interview.answer: A single font file with axes for weight, width or slant, so the page can request intermediate values without downloading several files.

interview.q: What does font-style control?
interview.answer: Whether the face is normal, italic or oblique, and the browser may synthesise a slant if the family lacks a real italic.

interview.q: Why use a type scale instead of arbitrary sizes?
interview.answer: A small set of related sizes creates hierarchy and rhythm, while one-off font sizes make the page look uneven and hard to maintain.

interview.q: Why express type sizes in rem?
interview.answer: rem follows the reader's root preference, so the whole scale grows together when the default font size is increased.

interview.q: What does line-height: normal mean?
interview.answer: The font's own recommended line spacing, which varies by typeface and is rarely the value a designer wants for body text.

interview.q: What is a readable measure?
interview.answer: Roughly 45 to 75 characters per line, often limited with ch, because lines that are too long or too short slow reading.

interview.q: What does letter-spacing change?
interview.answer: The space between characters; small positive values can help uppercase labels, while large values hurt word recognition.

interview.q: What does word-spacing change?
interview.answer: The space between words, which is rarely adjusted except for justified text or a specific display treatment.

interview.q: What does text-align affect?
interview.answer: The alignment of inline content inside its block, such as left, right, center or justify, not the position of the block itself.

interview.q: How do you remove an underline from a link accessibly?
interview.answer: Remove it only when another clear affordance remains, and always keep a visible focus and hover state so the link is still recognisable.

interview.q: What does text-transform do?
interview.answer: It changes the rendered case without changing the underlying text, so uppercase labels remain readable to screen readers and copy-paste.

interview.q: How does text-shadow differ from box-shadow?
interview.answer: text-shadow follows the glyph shapes and takes no spread or inset value, while box-shadow follows the element's box.

interview.q: What does text-overflow require to work?
interview.answer: A single-line box with overflow hidden and white-space nowrap, otherwise the text wraps and there is no overflow to ellipsise.

interview.q: What does white-space control?
interview.answer: Whether whitespace collapses, wraps or is preserved, which decides if text stays on one line or breaks at spaces.

interview.q: What does overflow-wrap: anywhere do?
interview.answer: It allows a long unbreakable string to break at any point when needed, preventing it from forcing the container wider.

interview.q: How is word-break different from overflow-wrap?
interview.answer: word-break changes the language's normal breaking rules, while overflow-wrap only intervenes when a word would otherwise overflow.

interview.q: What does hyphens: auto do?
interview.answer: It lets the browser insert language-aware hyphenation at line ends, which can improve justification but needs the correct lang attribute.

interview.q: What does text-wrap: balance do?
interview.answer: It distributes lines evenly in a short block such as a heading, avoiding a single orphan word on the last line.

interview.q: What does font-variant control?
interview.answer: It selects alternate glyph sets such as small caps or old-style numerals, a higher-level switch than raw font features.

interview.q: How do you enable tabular numbers?
interview.answer: Use font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums so digits share a width, which keeps columns of figures aligned.

interview.q: How do you style a drop cap?
interview.answer: Use ::first-letter with a larger size and float, then check the line box so the cap does not collide with the first line.

interview.q: What is vertical rhythm?
interview.answer: A consistent baseline spacing derived from line-height, so headings, paragraphs and margins land on the same grid instead of drifting.

interview.q: How do you make type responsive without breakpoints?
interview.answer: Use clamp() with a viewport-relative middle value and a readable minimum and maximum, then test the extremes.

interview.q: Why cap fluid type with clamp()?
interview.answer: Without a maximum, headings become absurdly large on wide screens; without a minimum, body text becomes unreadable on small ones.

interview.q: What text spacing does WCAG expect?
interview.answer: Readers must be able to increase line height, paragraph spacing, letter spacing and word spacing without losing content or functionality.

interview.q: Why is text contrast more than a colour choice?
interview.answer: The final ratio depends on the actual background, overlays and states, so a colour that passes on white can fail on an image or a tinted card.

interview.q: How do web fonts affect performance?
interview.answer: They add requests and bytes, can delay text, and may cause layout shift when the fallback and web font have different metrics.

interview.q: Why use system fonts on some projects?
interview.answer: They load instantly, match the platform and avoid layout shift, which is often the better trade-off for utility interfaces.

interview.q: Why prefer SVG icons over an icon font?
interview.answer: SVG icons are individually accessible, styleable and crisp at any size, while icon fonts depend on private-use glyphs and can fail silently.

interview.q: What are fallback font metrics?
interview.answer: The measurements used to match a fallback closely to the web font, reducing the size and position shift when the real font swaps in.

interview.q: When should a font be self-hosted?
interview.answer: When the project needs control over privacy, caching and licensing, or the third-party font service is a performance or reliability risk.

interview.q: What does font-smoothing change?
interview.answer: It alters glyph antialiasing on some platforms, which can make text look thinner or heavier but is not a reliable cross-browser design control.

interview.q: How do you debug a typography problem?
interview.answer: Inspect the computed font family, size and line height, then check whether a fallback rendered, a rule was overridden, or the measure is wrong.

interview.q: What are OpenType features in CSS?
interview.answer: Optional glyph behaviours such as ligatures, fractions or stylistic sets, enabled with font-feature-settings or higher-level font-variant properties.

interview.q: Why limit a paragraph with ch rather than px?
interview.answer: ch scales with the font, so the measure stays proportional when the reader changes text size instead of becoming too wide or too narrow.
